category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary defining mechanism of action for corrosive substances on tissue?
back: A corrosive destroys the physical texture of any body tissue it contacts through direct chemical destruction.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the specific mechanism behind the blackening of tissue in sulfuric acid burns?
back: Sulfuric acid produces intense heat and dehydrates the tissue, causing carbonization (turning from gray to black).
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Locally it produces the sensation of heat followed by pain. It blackens the tissue before actual destruction. The change of color is from gray to black.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic skin staining of nitric acid burns vs. sulfuric acid burns.
back:
• Nitric Acid: Yellow to brown stains.
• Sulfuric Acid: Gray to black (carbonized) stains.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, later turns brown.] Page 176 (Book Page): [Sulfuric acid... change of color is from gray to black.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why is pain often disproportionately low in severe carbolic acid (phenol) burns?
back: Phenol possesses local anesthetic properties that produce numbness, masking the actual extent of tissue destruction.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Skin surface shows burns but pain is not proportionate to extent of burn because of its anesthetic properties.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What local chemical reaction occurs when strong alkalis are ingested into the stomach?
back: Alkalis cause intense irritation and a frothy reaction when they encounter gastric hydrochloric acid.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Vomiting is copious showing frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What are the three primary clinical indicators of corrosive ingestion identified on the body?
back:
• Corrosion on lips/tongue/throat
• Mucous in vomitus
• Staining on the chin or groins from dribbling.
citation: Page 162 (Book Page): [Presence of corrosion on lips, tongue or in throat. mucous in vomits indicate corrosive poisoning.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: How does the volatility of a corrosive affect its primary site of development?
back: Volatile corrosives (like ammonia or fuming nitric acid) additionally target the respiratory tract and eyes through inhalation.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Being a fuming acid, it especially affects the respiratory tract... Ammonia emits fumes, which intensely affect eyes and respiratory tract.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Distinguish the vomitus appearance in mineral acid vs. strong alkali poisoning.
back:
• Mineral Acids: Dark brown (altered blood) or 'coffee ground'.
• Strong Alkalis: Initially white, later becoming black.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [blood stained or of dark brown color due to presence of altered blood.] Page 177 (Book Page): [The vomit is first of white color, later becomes black.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the systemic mechanism of death following the absorption of oxalic acid?
back: It depresses the central nervous system, leading to paralysis of vital medullary centers (respiratory/cardiac).
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Systemic effects after absorption are depression of central nervous system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What are the three most common external 'dribbling' sites for corrosive lesions?
back:
1. Lips
2. Lateral aspects of the chin
3. Groins/thighs (when solution falls while sitting).
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin... then on groins and thighs.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of action for strong corrosive substances?
back: Corrosives produce tissue damage by destroying the actual texture of any tissue they encounter through immediate chemical destruction upon contact.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the specific mechanism of sulfuric acid on skin appearance.
back: It blackens the tissue before actual destruction, causing a characteristic color change from gray to black.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): It blackens the tissue before actual destruction. The change of color is from gray to black.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the staining mechanism of Nitric acid versus Sulfuric acid burns.
back: Nitric acid produces yellow stains that later turn brown, whereas Sulfuric acid typically causes blackening (carbonization).
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): Skin stains are yellow in color, later tums brown.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: A patient presents with yellow skin burns and severe choking. What is the likely corrosive mechanism?
back: Nitric acid exposure. Its volatility results in respiratory tract damage (choking) alongside its characteristic yellow skin corrosion.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): Nitric acid ... being more volatile has stronger effects on the respiratory tract. Skin stains are yellow in color.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why is pain often disproportionate to the extent of burn in Phenol poisoning?
back: Phenol acts as a protoplasmic poison with anesthetic properties, causing initial burning followed by numbness that masks tissue destruction.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): but pain is not proportionate to extent of burn because of its anesthetic properties. It acts as a protoplasmic poison.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What external sites define the distribution of ingested liquid corrosives in a seated patient?
back: Corrosion typically appears on the lips, lateral aspects of the chin (dribbling), and the groins or thighs.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): local effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin ... and then on groins by dribbled solution when it falls down on thighs.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Explain why alkalis like Caustic Soda are particularly damaging to the gastrointestinal tract.
back: Alkalis increase the permeability of the gastrointestinal mucosa, facilitating deeper penetration and more extensive tissue liquefaction compared to acids.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): Strong alkalis ... more so on the mucous membranes. ... in turn increases permeability of the gastrointestinal tract.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Differentiate the respiratory mechanism of Hydrochloric acid from Sulfuric acid.
back: Hydrochloric acid is fuming and volatile, primarily attacking respiratory passages; Sulfuric acid is non-volatile and causes deeper localized tissue blackening.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): Sulfuric acid is one of the strongest non-volatile mineral acids. Page 177 (Book Page): Being a fuming acid, it [Hydrochloric] specially affects the respiratory tract.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What systemic loop follows the local corrosive action of Oxalic Acid?
back: After absorption, it enters the circulation to depress the CNS, causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital medullary centers.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): Systemic effects after absorption are depression of CNS system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the defining internal anatomic result of severe stomach corrosion?
back: Corrosion of the gastric mucosa eventually produces perforation, leading to the leakage of contents and subsequent peritonitis.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): eventually produces perforation of stomach and first part of duodenum.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What defines a corrosive or chemical lesion to body tissues?
back:
- Contact with strong acids or alkalis.
- Destruction of the physical texture and structure of the contacted tissue.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Corrosive lesion to the skin and internal lining surfaces of the body organs occurs, when a strong acid or alkali come in contact. Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the primary internal and external vulnerable sites for chemical burns?
back:
- External: Face, hands, and feet.
- Internal: Mucous membranes of the stomach, intestines, and respiratory passages.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Vulnerable sites externally are exposed areas of the body-such as skin of face, hands and feet and internally mucous membranes of stomach, intestines and respiratory passages.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the skin staining colors produced by Sulfuric acid versus Nitric acid.
back:
- Sulfuric acid: Gray to black.
- Nitric acid: Yellow, later turning brown.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [The change of color is from gray to black. (Sulfuric acid)] Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, which later turns brown.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the external clinical presentation of a corrosive ingested in a sitting position.
back:
- Staining on lips and lateral aspects of the chin.
- Dribbling effects visible on the groins and thighs.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If ingested while in. sitting position, external effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on groins by dribbled solution when it falls down on thighs.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Why is pain often disproportionately low in Carbolic acid (Phenol) burns?
back: - Phenol possesses local anesthetic properties that numb the area despite tissue destruction.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Skin surface shows burns but pain is not proportionate to extent of burn because of its anesthetic properties.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the diagnostic significance of a litmus test on a chemical lesion?
back: - Testing the periphery of the lesion identifies if the causative agent was acidic or alkaline.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Litmus reaction at the periphery of the lesion will be in accordance with type of corrosive used.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What characteristic clinical reaction occurs when strong alkalis reach the stomach?
back: - Copious vomiting with a frothy reaction caused by mixing with gastric hydrochloric acid.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Vomiting is copious showing frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the respiratory findings in a victim exposed to fuming (volatile) corrosive acids.
back:
- Intense irritation of eyes.
- Choking and damage to the nasal mucosa and lung tissue.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If corrosive substance has fuming property... may gain entry into respiratory passages by inhalation, affecting nasal mucosa and lungs. Effect on respiration is choking.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the immediate effect of Oxalic acid on the central nervous system?
back: - Rapid depression of vital centers, leading to unconsciousness, weak pulse, and prostration.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Systemic effects after absorption are depression of central nervous system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers. The pulse becomes weak... the person rapidly becomes prostrated.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What physical feature characterizes a chemical burn as an ante-mortem injury?
back: - The presence of a defined ulcer surrounded by an acute inflammatory reaction.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [The lesion also acquire the shape of an ulcer having acute inflammatory reaction.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary defining mechanism of action for corrosive chemical substances?
back:
- Direct destruction of the tissue texture upon contact
- Localized inflammatory reaction and ulceration
- Potential systemic effects following absorption
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets. Some corrosive substances have additional systemic effects after their absorption.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the specific mechanism of tissue damage caused by sulfuric acid contact.
back:
- Initial sensation of intense heat and pain
- Dehydration and destruction of tissue
- Color change from gray to black (vitriolage)
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Locally it produces the sensation of heat followed by pain. It blackens the tissue before actual destruction. The change of color is from gray to black. It is also known as oil of vitriol]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why is pain often disproportionate to the severity of a Carbolic acid (Phenol) burn?
back:
- Phenol possesses inherent anesthetic properties
- Initial burning sensation is rapidly followed by numbness
- This masks the extent of deep tissue destruction
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Local application causes burning sensation followed by numbness. Skin surface shows burns but pain is not proportionate to extent of burn because of its anesthetic properties.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: In a clinical scenario of oral corrosive ingestion, why are the groins and thighs frequently burned?
back:
- Dribbling effect of the liquid from the chin
- Gravity-driven flow when the victim is in a sitting position
- Lack of immediate neutralization on skin surfaces
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If ingested while in sitting position, local effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on groins and thighs by the dribbled solution when it falls down on them.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of death in systemic Hydrocyanic acid poisoning.
back:
- Acts as a protoplasmic poison
- Inhibits the enzyme cytochrome oxidase
- Prevents cellular oxygen utilization (internal asphyxia)
citation: Page 187 (Book Page): [Remote action after its absorption is at the level of the cell. It acts as protoplasmic poison and inhibits enzyme cytochrome oxidase and prevents consumption of oxygen by the cell. Interference with cellular respiration produces death of the cell.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What are the macroscopic diagnostic criteria for oral mineral acid burns?
back:
- Corrosion/staining of lips and mouth
- Dark brown vomit (altered blood)
- Potential gastric perforation and peritonitis
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Internal effects are on cavity of mouth, throat and upper alimentary tract... Vomiting may occur... blood stained or of dark brown color due to the presence of altered blood.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: How does the mechanism of Nitric acid fumes differ from liquid contact?
back:
- Liquid causes yellow skin staining (turning brown)
- Volatile fumes cause intense irritation and edema of the glottis
- Leads to acute respiratory obstruction and choking
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid behaves similar to sulfuric acid and being more volatile has stronger effects on the respiratory tract. Skin stains are yellow in color, which later turns brown.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Differentiate the local mechanism of death in corrosive ingestion from Oxalic acid's systemic mechanism.
back:
- Local: Massive corrosion and perforation of the stomach/intestine
- Systemic: Depression of the central nervous system and paralysis of vital medullary centers
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Remote systemic effects after absorption are depression of central nervous system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers... pulse becomes weak... he dies in ten, twenty or thirty minutes.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind 'rice-water' stools in acute chemical arsenic poisoning.
back:
- Massive transudation of plasma into the intestinal lumen
- Direct mucosal irritation and tissue damage
- Stimulated peristalsis due to bulk effect of fluids
citation: Page 172 (Book Page): [Bulk effect of transudes into the lumen of small intestine together with mucosal irritation and damage, which stimulates peristalsis leading to characteristic rice-water stools.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Which specific ocular mechanism occurs in chemical burns caused by ammonia exposure?
back:
- Intense irritation of mucous membranes
- Fuming action causes rapid penetration and corneal damage
- Often accompanied by glottic edema
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Ammonia emits fumes, which intensely affect eyes and respiratory tract. It may also produce edema of glottis.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Define the core mechanism of a corrosive or chemical lesion.
back: The strong corrosive substance destroys the texture of the body tissue it meets upon contact.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Corrosive lesion to the skin and internal lining surfaces of the body organs occurs, when a strong acid or alkali come in contact. Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What determines the varied clinical appearance of chemical burns?
back:
Appearance depends on:
- Amount of substance taken
- Duration of contact
- Concentration of the solution
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Affects vary with amount taken, duration of contact and concentration of the solution.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the local vs systemic mechanisms of corrosive substances.
back: Most act locally by destroying tissue texture; however, some organic acids cause additional systemic effects after absorption.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Some corrosive substances have additional systemic effects after their absorption.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the specific mechanism of Sulfuric Acid on tissues.
back: It is a potent nonvolatile mineral acid that blackens tissue, changing the color from gray to black.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Sulfuric acid is one of the strongest nonvolatile mineral acids... It blackens the tissue before actual destruction. The change of color is from gray to black.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Explain the systemic mechanism of Oxalic Acid after its local corrosive action.
back: After absorption, it depresses the central nervous system, eventually causing paralysis of vital medullary centers.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Systemic effects after absorption are depression of central nervous system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What are the diagnostic external burn sites for a victim sitting during ingestion?
back: Irritant or corrosive dribbling causes burns on the lips, lateral chin, groins, and thighs.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If ingested while in sitting position, external effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on groins by the dribbled solution when it falls down on thighs.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: How does the fuming property of Nitric Acid facilitate lung damage?
back: Being volatile, its fumes are inhaled, causing intense damage to the respiratory passages and lung tissue.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid... being more volatile has stronger effects on the respiratory tract.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why does Carbolic Acid (Phenol) cause deep burns with disproportionately low pain?
back: It acts as a protoplasmic poison with anesthetic properties, causing local numbness despite deep tissue destruction.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Local application causes burning sensation followed by numbness. Skin surface shows burns but pain is not proportionate to extent of burn because of its anesthetic properties.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Detail the secondary anatomical complications of surviving a corrosive ingestion.
back: Survivors often develop esophageal, laryngeal, and pyloric stenoses, as well as pulmonary fibrosis.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If the patient survives, the residual effects of such corrosions are esophageal, laryngeal and pyloric stenoses and fibrosis of the lungs.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: List the primary external anatomic targets of strong chemical corrosives.
back: The most vulnerable exposed areas are the skin of the face, hands, and feet.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Vulnerable sites externally are exposed areas of the body such as skin of face, hands and feet]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary pathological mechanism of a corrosive chemical burn?
back:
- Destroys the texture of the tissue it meets upon contact.
- Causes massive corrosion and localized inflammatory reactions.
- May produce systemic toxic effects if absorbed.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets. Some corrosive substances have additional systemic effects after their absorption.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the characteristic skin color changes associated with Sulfuric acid burns.
back:
- Initially produces a sensation of heat and pain.
- The skin color changes from gray to black (charring).
- Also known as 'Oil of Vitriol'.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It blackens the tissue before actual destruction. The change of color is from gray to black. It is also known as oil of vitriol]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Differentiate the skin staining of Nitric acid from Sulfuric acid burns.
back:
- Nitric acid: Produces yellow stains that later turn brown.
- Sulfuric acid: Produces gray to black charring.
- Nitric acid is more volatile and affects the respiratory tract more severely.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid behaves similar to sulfuric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, and later turns brown.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What defines 'Oil of Vitriol' throwing in a clinical forensic scenario?
back:
- Use of strong Sulfuric acid to cause facial disfiguration.
- Usually motivated by jealousy or criminal intent.
- Results in deep tissue destruction and permanent scarring.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It is also known as oil of vitriol and is thrown for disfiguration of face usually in cases of jealousy.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: How is the causative agent identified at the periphery of a chemical burn?
back:
- Using the Litmus reaction.
- The reaction at the periphery of the lesion will be acidic or alkaline depending on the type of corrosive used.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Litmus reaction at the periphery of the lesion will be in accordance with type of corrosive used.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: List the external diagnostic hallmarks of ingested fuming corrosives.
back:
- Corrosion of lips, angles of mouth, and chin (dribbling marks).
- Involvement of the nasal openings due to fuming properties.
- Accompanying staining on clothes.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Internal effects are on cavity of mouth, throat... If corrosive substance has fuming property, it may additionally affect nose and eyes externally]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Why is gastric lavage generally avoided in strong mineral acid ingestion?
back:
- Risk of gastric or esophageal perforation.
- The corrosive may have already thinned the walls through massive destruction.
- Lavage could leak acid into the peritoneal cavity.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It is done nearly in all cases of ingested poison except when contraindicated as in poisoning by corrosive.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the appearance of the vomit in acid versus alkali ingestion.
back:
- Acids: Blood-stained or dark brown (altered blood); shows effervescence on contact with earth.
- Alkalis: Copious, frothy (reaction with gastric HCl), initially white then black.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [The vomit will also show effervescence on contact with earth in case of acid... Vomiting is copious showing frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the specific systemic effects of absorbed Phenol (Carbolic acid).
back:
- Depresses central nervous system vital centers.
- Specifically causes cardiac and respiratory medullary failure.
- Excreted in urine, which darkens on exposure to air.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [It acts locally and has systemic effects as well... It depresses both cardiac and medullary centers especially cardiac and respiratory.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the most common vulnerable sites for internal chemical burns?
back:
- Mucous membranes of the mouth and throat.
- Esophagus (gullet).
- Stomach and first part of the duodenum.
- Respiratory passages (if fuming).
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Vulnerable sites... internally mucous membranes of stomach, intestines and respiratory passages.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary defining action of a corrosive substance on human tissue?
back: It destroys the texture of the tissue it meets through direct chemical contact.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets, Some corrosive substances have additional systemic effects after their absorption.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the initial local mechanism of action for strong mineral acids.
back: They cause rapid dehydration and coagulation of tissue proteins at the site of contact.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat... It includes all types of thermal lesions... followed by development of areas of coagulation, of both skin and deeper tissue.] Note: Page 175 (Book Page)-177 clarifies mineral acids (sulfuric, nitric, hydrochloric) act by destroying tissue texture.

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Differentiate the skin discoloration produced by sulfuric acid vs. nitric acid burns.
back: Sulfuric acid changes tissue color from gray to black; Nitric acid produces yellow stains that later turn brown.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Sulfuric acid... It blackens the tissue before actual destruction. The change of color is from gray to black.] Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, which later turns brown.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why does ingested strong mineral acid produce 'dark brown' vomit and floor effervescence?
back: The color results from altered blood; effervescence occurs when the acid reacts with carbonates in the earth/floor.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [The vomit will also show effervescence on contact with earth in case of acid. ...dark brown color due to the presence of altered blood.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
coreConcept: Systemic Toxic Mechanism of Oxalic Acid
front: Q: What is the systemic mechanism of death in acute oxalic acid poisoning?
back: It depresses the central nervous system, leading to unconsciousness and eventual paralysis of vital medullary centers.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Systemic effects after absorption are depression of central nervous system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: List the three vulnerable body regions for external and internal corrosive burns.
back: 1. Exposed skin (face/hands/feet); 2. Alimentary tract mucous membranes (mouth/stomach); 3. Respiratory passages.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Vulnerable sites externally are exposed areas of the body such as skin of face, hands and feet and internally mucous membranes of stomach, intestines and respiratory passages.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why does carbolic acid (phenol) cause numbness despite severe tissue destruction?
back: It possesses local anesthetic properties that desensitize the area even while acting as a protoplasmic poison.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Skin surface shows burns but pain is not proportionate to extent of burn because of its anesthetic properties.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the progression from corrosive ingestion to fatal secondary peritonitis.
back: The corrosive produces full-thickness necrosis or perforation of the stomach/duodenum, leaking contents into the peritoneal cavity.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Eventually produces perforation of stomach and first part of duodenum and peritoneal damage.] Page 177 (Book Page): [There may be perforation of stomach, leading to the leakage of the corrosive into the peritoneal cavity resulting in peritonitis.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the physiological effect of inhaling fuming corrosive acid vapors?
back: It causes intense irritation of the nasal mucosa, glottic edema, choking, and direct damage to lung tissue.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [When inhaled, lung tissue is badly damaged. ...Effect on respiration is choking. ...Intensely affects eyes and respiratory tract.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What secondary anatomical changes occur if a patient survives the acute phase of corrosive ingestion?
back: Development of esophageal, laryngeal, or pyloric stenoses and fibrosis of the lungs.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If the patient survives, the residual effects of such corrosions are esophageal, laryngeal and pyloric stenoses and fibrosis of the lungs.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism by which corrosive substances damage body tissues?
back:
• Direct destruction of the tissue texture on contact.
• Massive corrosion resulting in inflammatory reactions.
• Some agents cause additional systemic effects after absorption.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets. Some corrosive substances have additional systemic effects after their absorption.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What specific tissue change causes the characteristic color in sulfuric acid burns?
back:
• Dehydration and coagulation of tissue proteins.
• Conversion of hemoglobin into acid hematin.
• Blackens the tissue before actual death occurs.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It blackens the tissue before actual death. . . The change of color is from gray to black.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: How do the skin stains of nitric acid and sulfuric acid burns differ?
back:
• Nitric acid: Yellow stains that later turn brown.
• Sulfuric acid: Gray to black charring/blackening.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, later turns brown. . . Sulfuric acid... blackens the tissue...]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What is the mechanism of injury for fuming acids entering the respiratory tract?
back:
• Direct inhalation of volatile vapors.
• Causes acute irritation and corrosion of nasal mucosa/lungs.
• Results in choking and chemical pneumonia.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If corrosive substance has fuming property, it may additionally affect nose, eyes externally and may gain entry into respiratory passages by inhalation... Effect on respiration is choking.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the biochemical reaction between ingested strong alkalis and gastric acid.
back:
• Produces a frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid.
• Causes local irritation and massive mucous secretion.
• Increases the density of the gastrointestinal tract damage.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Strong alkalis... produce frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid. Local irritation causes secretion of mucous, which in turn increases density of the gastrointestinal tract and cause the damage.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What are the defining visual criteria for a corrosive lesion on exposed skin?
back:
• Range from erythema to massive tissue destruction.
• Presentation of an ulcer with acute inflammatory reaction.
• Specific staining on skin/clothes related to the corrosive type.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Lesion has varied appearance range from simple erythema... to massive corrosion of the tissues, which finally may acquire the shape of an ulcer having acute inflammatory reaction. The lesion also shows staining on the skin and the clothes related to the type of corrosive.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: Why do certain ingested corrosives cause external damage to the chin and groins?
back:
• Occurs due to the 'dribbling effect' of the liquid during ingestion.
• Irritant fluid follows gravity along body surfaces.
• Causes streaks of corrosion on the chin, neck, and thighs.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If ingested while in sitting position, external effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on groins by dribbled solution when it falls down on thighs.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What dual mechanisms lead to death in carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning?
back:
• Local: Skin burns and numbness (anesthetic property).
• Systemic: Depression/paralysis of central respiratory and cardiac medullary centers.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Phenol... acts locally and has systemic effects as well. . . systemic effects are mainly on central nervous system. It depresses both heart and medullary centers especially cardiac and respiratory.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: What physiological loop leads to the chronic complication of stenosis after corrosive ingestion?
back:
• Tissue destruction is followed by the process of repair.
• Resultant healing leads to esophageal, laryngeal, or pyloric strictures.
• Inhalation leads to lung fibrosis.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If the patient survives, the residual effects of such corrosions are esophageal, laryngeal and pyloric stenoses and fibrosis of the lungs.]

category: Explain mechanism of development of chemical burns
front: Q: How is the corrosive agent type determined using the litmus reaction?
back:
• Litmus reaction is tested at the periphery of the burn lesion.
• Indicates if the agent was acidic (mineral acids) or alkaline (caustic sodas).
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Litmus reaction at the periphery of the lesion will be in accordance with type of corrosive used.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Define a corrosive or chemical lesion.
back: The destruction of tissue texture upon contact with a strong acid or alkali, resulting in ulceration and acute inflammatory reaction.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): Corrosive lesion to the skin and internal lining surfaces of the body organs occurs, when a strong acid or alkali come in contact. Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the mechanism of action for corrosive substances on tissues?
back: Direct chemical destruction of tissue structure followed by inflammatory edema; systemic effects may follow absorption.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets, Some corrosive substances have additional systemic effects after their absorption.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the skin staining of Sulfuric Acid vs. Nitric Acid.
back:
• Sulfuric Acid: Gray to black.
• Nitric Acid: Yellow, turning brown later.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): Sulfuric acid... The change of color is from gray to black... Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, which later turns brown.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the clinical distribution of 'dribbling' marks in corrosive ingestion.
back: Corrosive marks appear on the lips, lateral aspects of the chin, and often on the groins/thighs where the fluid fell.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): If ingested while in sitting position, external effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on groins by dribbled solution when it falls down on thighs.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What specific chemical antidote is used for Oxalic acid burns/ingestion?
back: Calcium salts (e.g., lime water), which react to form insoluble calcium oxalate.
citation: Page 169 (Book Page): Calcium salt administered in case of oxalic acid poisoning reacts with it to yield poorly soluble calcium oxalate, which largely passes through intestine without being absorbed.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: List the external hallmarks of fuming (volatile) acid ingestion.
back: Corrosion involving the nose, eyes, and respiratory tract due to inhaled vapors, in addition to oral burns.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): If corrosive substance has fuming property, it may additionally affect nose and eyes externally and may gain entry into respiratory passages by inhalation, affecting nasal mucosa and lungs.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the delayed residual effects of surviving a corrosive burn?
back: Development of stenoses (esophageal, laryngeal, or pyloric) and pulmonary fibrosis.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): If the patient survives, the residual effects of such corrosions are esophageal, laryngeal and pyloric stenoses and fibrosis of the lungs.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: How is a true corrosive burn differentiated from postmortem skin slip?
back: Corrosive burns show vital reaction (hyperemia and inflammation) at the margins, which is absent in postmortem artifacts.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): The base moist and showing no vital reaction are postmortem blisters and skin-slip... Litmus reaction at the periphery of the lesion will be in accordance with type of corrosive used.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the systemic effects of Carbolic acid (Phenol) absorption.
back: Depression of central nervous system centers (cardiac/respiratory), hypotension, and urine that darkens on exposure.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): It acts locally and has systemic effects as well... It depresses both heart and medullary centers especially cardiac and respiratory... Urine darkens on exposure.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What visual evidence on the stomach mucosa suggests Sulfuric acid ingestion?
back: A typical velvety appearance with dark brown or black discoloration due to carbonization and altered blood.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): The change of color is from gray to black... The vomit will also show effervescence on contact with earth in case of acid... blackens the tissue before actual destruction.

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What defines a corrosive lesion in forensic medicine?
back: Destruction of tissue texture upon contact with a strong acid or alkali, creating ulceration with inflammatory reaction.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Corrosive lesion to the skin and internal lining surfaces of the body organs occurs, when a strong acid or alkali come in contact. Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and appearance of internal corrosive injury in the stomach.
back: Produces intense pain and vomiting of dark brown or blood-stained fluid (altered blood), potentially leading to perforation.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Internal effects are on cavity of mouth, throat, and upper alimentary tract. Pain is intense in stomach and upper intestine. ... Vomiting may occur, which has the smell of the ingested corrosive, blood stained or of dark brown color due to the presence of altered blood.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic skin stains produced by Nitric and Sulfuric acid.
back:
• Nitric Acid: Yellow stains (turning brown later).
• Sulfuric Acid: Gray to black charring.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Sulfuric acid... The change of color is from gray to black. ... Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, which later tums brown.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: A victim has skin burns with local numbness and dark urine. Which substance is suspected?
back: Carbolic acid (Phenol), known for its local anesthetic properties and darkening of urine upon exposure.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Carbolic acid (phenol)... Local application causes burning sensation followed by numbness. ... It is excreted in urine and breath, which smells of carbolic acid. Urine darkens on exposure.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Why is gastric lavage generally contraindicated in corrosive poisoning?
back: The softened, corroded walls of the esophagus and stomach are highly susceptible to mechanical perforation.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It is done nearly in all cases of ingested poison except when contraindicated as in poisoning by corrosive.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the diagnostic features of alkali-induced vomiting?
back: Initially copious and frothy (reaction with stomach acid), appearing white, then turning black due to tissue destruction.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Vomiting is copious showing frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid. The vomit is first of white color and later becomes black.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: How is the 'dribbling effect' used to determine a victim's posture during corrosive ingestion?
back: Corrosive marks on the chin and lateral neck indicate the victim was in a sitting or upright position.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If ingested while in sitting position, external effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on neck]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Differentiate between the local and systemic actions of Oxalic Acid.
back:
• Local: Weak corrosive, acidic taste, gastric burning.
• Systemic: CNS depression, prostration, and vital center paralysis.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Oxalic acid has both local and systemic action. It acts as weak corrosive... Tastes acidic in mouth and causes burning sensation... Remote action after absorption are depression of CNS system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What specific respiratory effect occurs when a fuming corrosive like ammonia is inhaled?
back: Intense irritation leading to choking, edema of the glottis, and potential chemical pneumonia.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If corrosive substance has fuming property, it may additionally affect nose externally... Effect on respiration is choking. ... Page 177 (Book Page): Ammonia emits fumes, which intensely affect eyes and respiratory tract.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Which anatomical sites are most vulnerable to external chemical burns?
back: Exposed body areas, specifically the face, hands, and feet.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Vulnerable sites externally are exposed areas of the body such as skin of face, hands and feet]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Define the primary action of a corrosive substance in chemical burns.
back: A corrosive substance destroys the texture of the living tissue it meets on contact, including skin or internal mucous membranes.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological mechanism of respiratory damage by fuming acids?
back: Fuming acids emit vapors that, when inhaled, cause intense irritation, choking, and direct damage to lung tissue or nasal mucosa.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Ammonia emits fumes, which intensely eyes and respiratory tract. ... Being a fuming acid, it specially affects the respiratory tract.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Contrast the appearance of vomit in mineral acid versus strong alkali ingestion.
back:
• Mineral Acid: Blood-stained or dark brown (altered blood).
• Strong Alkali: Copious, frothy, initially white, then turning black.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Vomiting is copious showing frothy reaction... The vomit is first of white color, later becomes black. ... blood stained or of dark brown color due to the presence of altered blood.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the clinical presentation of 'Vitriolage' involving concentrated sulfuric acid.
back:
• Gray to black tissue discoloration.
• Intense pain followed by deep ulceration.
• Massive disfiguration, typically of the face.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It blackens the tissue before actual death... The change of color is from gray to black. It is also known as oil of vitriol and is thrown for disfiguration of face]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the specific chemical color change associated with nitric acid burns?
back: Nitric acid produces yellow stains on the skin, which eventually turn brown over time.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Nitric acid... Skin stains are yellow in color, later turns brown.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: List the hallmark diagnostic features of Carbolic acid (Phenol) contact.
back:
• Local burning sensation.
• Rapid local numbness (anesthetic property).
• Urine that darkens upon exposure to air.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Local application produces burning sensation followed by numbness. ... It is excreted in urine and breath... Urine darkens on exposure.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Explain the 'dribbling effect' seen in corrosive ingestion cases.
back: Liquid corrosives often cause linear burn marks on the lateral aspects of the chin and the groins (from falling off the thighs) while sitting.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If ingested while in sitting position, external effects are on lips, lateral aspects of chin due to irritant and dribbling effect and then on groins by dribbled solution]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: How does the systemic action of Oxalic acid differ from its local corrosive effects?
back: Locally it acts as a weak corrosive; systemically, it depresses the CNS, causing rapid prostration, irregular respiration, and cardiovascular collapse.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Organic systemic effects after absorption are depression of CNS system finally causing unconsciousness and paralysis of vital centers. ... In whatever concentration the poison is ingested the person rapidly becomes prostrated.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: Describe the physiological response of capillaries to asphyxiant chemical burns.
back: Anoxia causes capillary dilatation, increased permeability, plasma transudation (edema), and eventual rupture (Tardieu's spots/petechiae).
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Anoxia also increases permeability of capillary wall forcing fluid out into the tissue spaces... eventually rupture causing blood leaks of small size out of these vessels. These petechial hemorrhages... are identified with his name as Tardieu’s spots.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What defines the microscopic 'vital reaction' in an ante-mortem chemical burn?
back: The presence of leucocyte infiltration at the injury site and increased enzyme activity (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) at the burn periphery.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Microscopy: Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration... Histo-chemistry at the periphery of the burnt skin indicates increased enzymes reaction]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of action for corrosive chemical burns?
back: Corrosives destroy the texture of the tissue they encounter. They produce local destruction to skin and internal lining surfaces, typically resulting in ulcer formation and acute inflammatory reactions.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the internal effects of ingesting a corrosive chemical?
back: * Intense pain in the stomach and upper intestine. * Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). * Vomiting of blood-stained or dark brown "altered blood." * Potential perforation leading to peritonitis.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [Internal effects are on cavity of mouth, throat, and upper alimentary tract. Pain is intense in stomach and upper intestine... Vomiting may occur... blood stained or of dark brown color due to presence of altered blood.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: How do skin stains differ between sulfuric acid and nitric acid burns?
back: * Sulfuric Acid: Changes tissue color from gray to black (charring). * Nitric Acid: Stains are initially yellow, later turning brown.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [[Sulfuric acid] blackens the tissue... change of color is from gray to black. [Nitric acid] Skin stains are yellow in color, later tums brown.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: A suicidal patient presents with skin numbness and dark urine. Which corrosive is suspected?
back: Phenol (Carbolic Acid). It acts locally as an anesthetic causing numbness. Systemically, it depresses medullary centers and typically causes urine to darken upon exposure to air.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Local application causes burning sensation followed by numbness... It depresses both heart and medullary centers... Urine darkens on exposure. Phenol is the most common suicidal poison.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is the specific chemical antidote for oxalic acid poisoning and why?
back: Calcium salts. They react with oxalic acid to produce poorly soluble calcium oxalate, which passes through the intestine without being absorbed into the bloodstream.
citation: Page 169 (Book Page): [Calcium salt administered in case of oxalic acid poisoning reacts with it to yield poorly soluble calcium oxalate, which largely passes through intestine without being absorbed.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What is "Oil of Vitriol" and its common criminal use?
back: It is strong sulfuric acid. It is commonly thrown on the face to cause permanent disfigurement, an act typically associated with cases of jealousy (vitriolage).
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [It is also known as oil of vitriol and is thrown to cause disfiguration of face usually in cases of jealousy.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What clinical features distinguish strong alkali ingestion from acid ingestion?
back: Alkalis produce copious, frothy vomiting due to the reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid. The vomit is initially white but later turns black.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [Vomiting is copious showing frothy reaction with gastric hydrochloric acid. The vomit is first of white color, later becomes black.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: A patient dies quickly with an imperceptible pulse and clammy skin. Diagnosis?
back: Acute Oxalic Acid poisoning. It is characterized by an abrupt onset, rapid prostration, and medullary paralysis, making the pulse weak or imperceptible within minutes.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [In whatever concentration the poison is ingested, the person rapidly becomes prostrated... pulse becomes weak, irregular and eventually imperceptible... No disease begins so abruptly.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the systemic respiratory effects of absorbed phenol?
back: Phenol acts as a protoplasmic poison that depresses the medullary respiratory centers, leading to respiratory failure. The breath typically retains a characteristic carbolic odor.
citation: Page 177 (Book Page): [As a protoplasmic poison, the systemic effects are mainly on central nervous system. It depresses both heart and medullary centers especially cardiac and respiratory. It is excreted in urine and breath, which smells of carbolic acid.]

category: Describe chemical burns
front: Q: What are the chronic residual effects of surviving corrosive ingestion?
back: * Esophageal, laryngeal, and pyloric stenoses (strictures). * Permanent fibrosis of the lungs if the corrosive was inhaled.
citation: Page 176 (Book Page): [If the patient survives, the residual effects of such corrosions are esophageal, laryngeal and pyloric stenoses and fibrosis of the lungs.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: List the four classical general pathological findings in fatal asphyxia.
back:
- Generalized cyanosis
- Vascular congestion
- Edema of tissues and viscera
- Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots)
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What is the expected site of hypostasis in a body suspended for a long period?
back:
- Lower limbs (stocking distribution)
- Hands (glove distribution)
- Tip of the penis in males
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [In case dead body remains in hanging for some period, postmortem lividity will appear at an-area of neck above ligature mark and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Contrast the margins of antemortem bruises with postmortem pseudo-bruising.
back:
- Antemortem: Shows vital reaction (swelling, inflammation, cell infiltration).
- Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction; usually due to blood displacement by gas pressure.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Bruise (Antemortem): Shows vital reaction (swelling and inflammation)... Pseudo-bruising: lacks vital reaction.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Which specific gastrointestinal finding is characteristic in severe thermal burn autopsies?
back: Curling ulcers (acute stress ulcers) found in the gastric and duodenal mucosa.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the stomach mucosa appearance in acute arsenic poisoning.
back: A typical 'velvety' appearance due to intense inflammatory edema and redness, sometimes with adherent white oxide particles.
citation: Page 173 (Book Page): [The mucous membrane has a typical velvety appearance, buffed up by inflammatory edema. Stray particles of white oxide may remain adherent to the walls]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: List three macroscopic autopsy features of respired lungs (live birth).
back:
- Fill thoracic cavity and overlap heart
- Spongy consistency (crepitant)
- Rounded edges with mottled light/dark red color
citation: Page 99 (Book Page): [Breathed lung: Fill thoracic cavity fully, overlapping the heart, become spongy in consistency and crepitate. Their edges get rounded]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Distinguish the ligature mark of Hanging from Strangulation.
back:
- Hanging: Oblique, non-continuous (absent at knot), depth decreases toward knot.
- Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous, uniform depth around the neck.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Table 13.3: Hanging: Oblique, Incomplete... Strangulation: Horizontal, Complete, Uniform depth]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Where is a traumatic extradural hemorrhage most commonly located?
back: In the temporal fossa, resulting from rupture of the middle meningeal vessels.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What finding in bone marrow is sought to confirm antemortem drowning?
back: Presence of diatoms (microscopic algae) inside the central part of long bones like the femur.
citation: Page 161 (Book Page): [Two to three gm. of bone marrow is preserved... from the central part of a long bone, especially femur in case of drowning to detect the presence of diatoms.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Which internal finding confirms carbon monoxide poisoning during autopsy?
back: Bright cherry-red coloration of the blood, tissues, and internal organs.
citation: Page 188 (Book Page): [Carboxy-hemoglobin does not clot and retains its bright cherry red color. It is present in all body tissues and organs]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Define the core components of a Forensic Autopsy.
back:
Scrutiny of the corpse involving:
- External surface examination.
- Opening and inspection of three internal body cavities.
- Further laboratory analysis of body tissues/fluids (histology, biochemistry, and toxicology).
citation: Page 113 (Book Page): Forensic Autopsy is scrutiny of corpse which consists of external surface, three internal body cavities including contents after opening them and further examination of collected body tissues/other material for histology, biochemistry and toxicology.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and appearance of Tardieu’s spots.
back:
- Nature: Petechial hemorrhages from capillary rupture due to anoxia.
- Location: Commonly seen under serous coverings of internal organs (e.g., lungs, heart).
- Significance: Hallmark of mechanical asphyxia deaths.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): Capillaries eventually rupture causing blood leaks of small size out of these vessels. These petechial hemorrhages were noticed first by Tardieu and are identified with his name as Tardieu’s spots. They occur in the substance of the organs, but are more readily seen under their serous coverings.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Contrast medical autopsy objectives with forensic autopsy.
back:
- Medical: Establish clinical diagnosis when investigations during life were inconclusive.
- Forensic: Establish cause and manner of death and rule out foul play in unnatural/suspicious deaths.
citation: Page 113 (Book Page): Medical autopsy is conducted for medical clinical to establish diagnosis in cases where clinical investigations during life of patient were inconclusive. Forensic autopsy is performed in pursuance of law to establish cause and manner of death and also to rule out foul play.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What does cherry-red hypostasis and globus pallidus softening indicate?
back:
- Diagnosis: Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning.
- Mechanism: Formation of stable carboxy-hemoglobin; brain changes occur due to severe anoxia.
citation: Page 188 (Book Page): Carboxy hemoglobin does not change its color for a long period... It softens globus pallidus, also seen in CO poisoning.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe internal autopsy findings in acute arsenic poisoning.
back:
- Gastric mucosa: Typical velvety appearance with inflammatory edema.
- Stomach wall: White oxide particles may adhere to erosions.
- Viscera: Acute fatty degeneration of liver, heart muscle, and kidneys.
citation: Page 173 (Book Page): Acute poisoning findings are that stomach and upper part of the small intestine are highly inflamed. The mucous membrane has a typical velvety appearance... The liver shows fatty degeneration... Heart muscle and kidney parenchyma show similar acute fatty degeneration.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: List the five general pathological findings of asphyxia.
back:
1. Generalized cyanosis.
2. Vascular congestion.
3. Edema of tissues/viscera.
4. Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu’s spots).
5. Persistent fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): Table 13.1; General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Define 'Marbling' as a postmortem finding.
back: A web-like pattern of dark brown or green veins on the skin. Caused by the reaction of escaping hemoglobin with hydrogen sulfide within the superficial vessels during early putrefaction.
citation: Page 136 (Book Page): The green color changes to blackish brown and veins in these areas become prominent and visible due to accumulation of gases in them due to decomposition and shows marbling stage.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Distinguish a pulmonary embolus from a postmortem clot at autopsy.
back:
- Embolus: Firm, dry, friable; takes the shape of the vein; shows transverse ridges (sausage-like).
- Postmortem Clot: Soft, smooth, shiny; purple or yellow ('chicken fat'); flabby and takes the shape of the vessel it is in.
citation: Page 121 (Book Page): An embolus is firm, has transverse ridges, coiled upon itself and generally of the size of the femoral vein. Postmortem clots... are soft, smooth, shiny and purple or yellow. When yellow in color, it is called chicken fat clot.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What is Adipocere and its autopsy significance?
back:
- Appearance: Yellowish-white, greasy, waxy substance.
- Process: Hydrogenation of body fats in moist, anaerobic environments.
- Significance: Preserves body features and injuries for years, aiding identification.
citation: Page 139 (Book Page): Adipocere formation... is a chemical change... consists of fatty acids... it has the greasy consistency of wax and fat... medco-legal importance... is in the preservation of facial anatomy of the deceased for years.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Which soft tissue organs are most resistant to putrefaction?
back:
- Male: Prostate gland.
- Female: Non-gravid uterus.
- Reason: These are compact, fibrous organs that remain identifiable even in advanced decomposition.
citation: Page 137 (Book Page): Prostate and non-gravid uterus being compact organs having dense fibrous tissue remains recognizable when decomposition of all other organs has far advanced.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Define Forensic Autopsy in the context of medico-legal practice.
back: The systematic scrutiny of a corpse involving examination of the external surface and all three internal body cavities to establish the cause, manner, and mode of death.
citation: Page 113 (Book Page): Forensic Autopsy is scrutiny of corpse which consists of external surface, three internal body cavities including contents after opening them and further examination of collected body tissues

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and diagnostic timing of Postmortem Lividity (Hypostasis).
back:
• Mechanism: Gravitational pooling of blood in dependent capillaries.
• Timing: Starts within 20-30 minutes; fully fixed in 6-12 hours.
citation: Page 133 (Book Page): red coloration on the dependent and unsupported portions of the body due to gravitational pooling of blood... starts in twenty to thirty minutes and usually gets fixed in six to twelve hours.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Contrast the ligature mark features of Hanging versus Ligature Strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique, in-continuous, high in the neck.
• Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous, middle of the neck, uniform depth.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): Hanging: High up in the neck, Oblique, Incomplete. Strangulation: Middle of neck, Horizontal, Complete, Uniform depth.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What is the 'Pugilistic Attitude' found in autopsies of severely burnt bodies?
back: A specific boxer-like posture caused by heat-induced protein coagulation and shortening of flexor muscles.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the defining internal findings in an acute Arsenic poisoning autopsy.
back: Stomach and small intestines show a 'velvety' appearance with inflammatory edema and adherent white oxide particles.
citation: Page 173 (Book Page): The mucous membrane has a typical velvety appearance, buffed up by inflammatory edema. Stray particles of white oxide may remain adherent to the walls

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are 'Tardieu’s Spots' and where are they classically found during autopsy?
back: Petechial hemorrhages caused by capillary rupture; most visible under the serous coverings of internal organs (e.g., lungs, heart).
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): These petechial hemorrhages... are identified with his name as Tardieu’s spots. They occur in the substance of the organs, but are more readily seen under their serous coverings.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe 'Marbling' and its cause during early decomposition.
back: A branching pattern of green/brown prominent veins caused by hemolysis and hydrogen sulfide reacting with hemoglobin.
citation: Page 136 (Book Page): disrupt blood causing hemolysis and staining the tissues... veins in these areas become prominent and visible... shows marbling stage.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: How is an ante-mortem abrasion differentiated from a post-mortem abrasion during autopsy?
back:
• Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (redness, exudation).
• Post-mortem: Lacks vital reaction; appears brown and parchment-like.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion... post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying has parchment appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: State the 'Rule of Thumb' for the duration of Rigor Mortis phases.
back:
• Phase 1 (Development): 4-6 hours.
• Phase 2 (Static/Stay): 4-6 hours.
• Phase 3 (Passing off): 4-6 hours.
citation: Page 134 (Book Page): average duration for its development, stay and passing off is four to six hours each in summer and ten to twelve hours in winter.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Name the primary external incision techniques for opening body cavities.
back:
1. Straight incision (chin to pubic symphysis).
2. Y-shaped incision (neck base/ears meeting at suprasternal notch).
citation: Page 119 (Book Page): Straight incision in the midline... from chin to pubic symphysis. Y-shaped incision extending obliquely down from the point just in front of the base of each ear to meet in the midline

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are the five classical general pathological findings in fatal asphyxia at autopsy?
back:
1. Generalized cyanosis
2. Vascular congestion
3. Edema of tissues/viscera
4. Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu’s spots)
5. Fluidity of blood
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Table 13.1: General pathological changes in asphyxia • Generalized cyanosis • Vascular congestion • Edema of the tissues and viscera • Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera • Fluidity of blood]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Explain the biochemical mechanism behind the development of rigor mortis.
back: Postmortem decomposition of ATP causes actin and myosin filaments to fuse into a rigid gel, creating irreversible muscular stiffening.
citation: Page 134 (Book Page): [After death, adenosine triphosphate of the muscles decomposes. Both the actin and myosin become stiff and get converted into a rigid gel... this state of muscles is called rigor mortis.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Contrast the ligature mark in hanging versus ligature strangulation at autopsy.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique, incomplete (interrupted at knot), depth decreases toward knot.
• Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous, uniform depth around neck.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Table 13.3... Hanging... Site: High up in the neck, Direction: Oblique, Extent: Incomplete... Strangulation... Site: Middle of neck, Direction: Horizontal, Extent: Complete]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Which specific findings on internal autopsy confirm a victim was alive during a fire?
back:
1. Black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi, and stomach.
2. Carboxy-hemoglobin levels exceeding 70% in blood/tissue.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood and other tissue like bone-marrow are strong evidence of an ante- mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are the internal autopsy hallmarks of fatal barbiturate poisoning?
back:
1. Softening of globus pallidus.
2. Punctate hemorrhages in brain white matter.
3. Dilated right heart with surface petechiae.
citation: Page 182 (Book Page): [It softens globus pallidus... Multiple punctate hemorrhages in white matter of brain... Right side of heart is dilated, filled with blood and shows hemorrhages on the surface.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Define a 'Negative Autopsy' and identify one possible physiological cause.
back:
Definition: A thorough examination failing to reveal a cause of death.
Possible Cause: Vagal inhibition/shock or cardiac arrhythmia.
citation: Page 126 (Book Page): [Such an autopsy is called negative autopsy... fails to establish the cause of death... Vagal inhibition, reflex cardiac arrest.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are the macro-anatomical features of a 'velvety' stomach in arsenic poisoning?
back: The gastric mucosa appears velvety due to intense inflammatory edema and hyperemia, occasionally with adherent white oxide particles.
citation: Page 173 (Book Page): [The mucous membrane has a typical velvety appearance, buffed up by inflammatory edema. Stray particles of white oxide may remain adherent to the walls.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: How is an extra-dural heat hematoma differentiated from a traumatic hematoma during autopsy?
back: Heat hematomas are light-colored, possess a honeycomb appearance, and are found immediately adjacent to external thermal skull burns.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [extra-dural heat hematoma, located in the immediate vicinity of external burn of head. The hematoma is light in color and has a honeycomb appearance.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the appearance of an antemortem pulmonary embolus in the calf veins.
back: The thrombus is firm, has transverse ridges, and 'pops out' as a solid sausage-like shape when the vein is transected.
citation: Page 121 (Book Page): [noticing a firm solidly structured thrombi Popping out as sausages from the transected vein. The postmortem clot being flabby does not pop out.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are the standard average weights for the heart and liver in a healthy male adult?
back:
• Heart: 275–325 grams.
• Liver: 1500–1700 grams.
citation: Page 122 (Book Page): [Chart 11.4... HEART Weight... 275-325 gm... LIVER Weight... 1500-1700 gm]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are the four classical internal autopsy signs of mechanical asphyxia?
back:
• Generalized visceral congestion
• Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu’s spots)
• Fluidity of blood
• Cyanosis and visceral edema
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Contrast the ligature mark characteristics between suicidal hanging and ligature strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique, discontinuous (absent at knot), situated high in the neck.
• Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous (encircling), situated in the middle of the neck.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Oblique, Incomplete, High up in the neck... Strangulation: Horizontal, Complete, Middle of neck]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What lung findings on autopsy indicate that a child was born alive?
back:
• Spongy, crepitant consistency
• Rounded edges
• Mottled light and dark red color
• Positive hydrostatic (flotation) test
citation: Page 99 (Book Page): [Breathed lung: Spongy, airless and crepitant; Edges rounded; Mottled and lighter; Flotation test Positive]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What autopsy findings prove a victim was alive during a fire?
back:
• Presence of black sooty particles in trachea or stomach.
• Carboxy-hemoglobin (CO) saturation levels above 10% in blood.
• Presence of vital reaction at burn margins.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 10% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante- mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic autopsy findings in a fatal opium (morphine) overdose.
back:
• Pinpoint pupils
• Acute visceral congestion and cyanosis
• Frothy mucus in air passages
• Fluid blood
citation: Page 182 (Book Page): [Autopsy findings are anoxic type such as acute cyanosis, congestion of internal organs, pinpoint pupils which go widely dilated as a terminal event]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Where is post-mortem hypostasis uniquely located in a body found hanging?
back:
• Hands and lower forearms
• Lower limbs (legs and feet)
• Tip of the penis (in males)
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [In case dead body remains in hanging for some period, postmortem lividity will appear at an-area of neck above ligature and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What local neck injuries are characteristic of manual strangulation (throttling) on autopsy?
back:
• Disc-like bruises from fingertips
• Linear or crescentic nail marks
• Fractured hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage
• Bruising of retropharyngeal soft tissues
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Specific findings depend upon... method of throttling... Bruises due to pressure of fingertips having adjacent nail marks are characteristic and present in front or both sides of the neck.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Contrast the autopsy appearance of extradural vs. subdural hemorrhages in head injuries.
back:
• Extradural: Biconvex/Lens-shaped, usually arterial (middle meningeal), associated with fractures.
• Subdural: Crescentic, usually venous (bridging veins), often follows contre-coup mechanism.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page)-91: [Extradural hemorrhage... ruptures them producing extradural hemorrhage. The most common site... is temporal fossa... Subdural hemorrhage... following rupture of a communicating cerebral vein at the site of contre-coup.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What pathognomonic autopsy sign indicates death due to air embolism?
back:
• Chain of bubbles in neck veins
• Frothy, churned-up blood in the right heart ventricle
• Air bubbles in coronary or cerebral arteries
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Postmortem appearance is characteristic showing presence of a chain of bubbles in the neck... its right side is filled with frothy blood.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the "Pugilistic Attitude" seen in burn victims at autopsy.
back:
• A boxer-like posture with flexed limbs.
• Caused by heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What are the three primary early external physical changes observed in a corpse?
back:
1. Fall of body temperature (Algor mortis).
2. Postmortem hypostasis (pooling of blood).
3. Development of Rigor mortis.
citation: Page 132 (Book Page): Early physical changes are due to stoppage of vital tissue responses and they are fall of body temperature, hypostasis, rigor mortis and changes in eye ball.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and defining pathological features of an ante-mortem bruise.
back: Sudden tissue indentation causes capillary rupture. Blood extravasates into surrounding tissues, showing vital reactions like swelling and inflammation.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil... Broken blood vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: How are antemortem burns distinguished from postmortem burns during autopsy?
back: Antemortem burns show vital reactions: line of reddening (1/4 inch width), leucocyte infiltration, and high peripheral enzyme reaction.
citation: Page 67 (Book Page): Antemortem burns show vital reaction... Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width... Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration.

category: Describe autopsy findings
front: Q: What unique autopsy findings characterize death from vagal shock in criminal abortion?
back: Absence of internal or external hemorrhage. No trauma except possible bruises on thighs. Resultant from sudden inhibitory cardiac arrest.
citation: Page 96 (Book Page): Death from vagal shock... Women dying of vagal shock show no internal and external hemorrhage... Many bruises on upper and medial part of thighs conforming interference.

category: Describe autopsy findings
